sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce \ours{}, a recurrent Transformer architecture with fixed-size memory that generalizes sliding-window attention while remaining parallelizable during training. \ours{} consists of two coupled models: a prefiller $Q$, which leverages full attention\footnote{In practice, we use interleaved full and sliding-window attention for $Q$, as this yields stronger performance. The essential requirement is that $Q$ be more expressive than $P$, with access to the full history.} to produce memory targets $m'_t$, and a decoder $P$, which uses only sliding-window attention and recurrent K/V injection to produce decoder memories $m_t$ for next-token prediction. We train \ours{} with a memory consistency loss that aligns $m_t$ with $m'_t$, allowing inference to use $P$ alone. Empirically, \ours{} improves validation loss and downstream pretraining benchmarks over sliding-window and latent recurrent transformer baselines. Moreover, sharing parameters between $P$ and $Q$ reduces parameter memory while preserving most of the gains.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce Maglev, recurrent Transformer architecture with fixed-size memory that generalizes sliding-window attention while remaining parallelizable during training. Maglev consists of two coupled models: prefiller Q, which leverages full attention1 to produce memory targets t, and decoder , which uses only sliding-window attention and recurrent K/V injection to produce decoder memories mt for next-token prediction. We train Maglev with memory consistency loss that aligns mt with t, allowing inference to use alone. Empirically, Maglev improves validation loss and downstream pretraining benchmarks over slidingwindow and latent recurrent transformer baselines. Moreover, sharing parameters between and reduces parameter memory while preserving most of the gains. Figure 1: Maglev: prefiller produces memory targets from the observed sequence, and decoder consumes the shifted t1 while predicting xt+1 and producing its own memory mt. The consistency loss aligns mt with t. At inference, the prefiller is discarded and the decoder runs recurrently using its own memories. In practice, we find that we could largely share parameters between and without degrading much performance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Transformers have simple memory strategy: keep every token. Full causal self-attention lets each prediction revisit the entire prefix, enabling powerful nonlinear retrieval, copying, and in-context computation [Vaswani et al., 2017]; its cost, however, grows with context. Sliding-window attention bounds both attention and KV-cache costs, but discards distant information and therefore provides no persistent long-term memory [Beltagy et al., 2020, Jiang et al., 2023]. Classical recurrent models such as LSTMs compress history with nonlinear token-wise updates, but propagate relatively small state sequentially, limiting both capacity and sequence parallelism [Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997]. Memory Transformers offer richer states, yet commonly update them only at segment or 1In practice, we use interleaved full and sliding-window attention for Q, as this yields stronger performance. The essential requirement is that be more expressive than , with access to the full history. Preprint. block boundaries, imposing an artificial granularity on memory [Dai et al., 2019, Rae et al., 2020, Hutchins et al., 2022, Bulatov et al., 2022]. Linear attention and state-space models remove these boundaries and parallelize token-wise recurrence, but do so through structured linear or affine updates [Katharopoulos et al., 2020, Gu et al., 2022, Gu and Dao, 2023, Dao and Gu, 2024, Liu et al., 2024a, Yang et al., 2024]. The missing piece is practical way to give nonlinear Transformer persistent memory that it can rewrite after every token. Goal: token-wise recurrent memory with parallel pretraining. We study language models with token-wise latent memory. After processing xt, the model writes latent memory vector mt and retains the bounded window Mt = {mtW +1, . . . , mt}, ignoring boundary effects. Writing all trainable parameters as Θ, the desired recurrent interface predicts the next token and writes the current memory from only recent token window and the preceding memory window, (1) pΘ(xt+1, mt xtW +1:t, Mt1). (2) practical token-wise memory model should combine three properties: Token-wise nonlinear memory. Unlike the structured, layer-local linear or affine updates of linear attention and state-space models [Katharopoulos et al., 2020, Gu et al., 2022, Gu and Dao, 2023, Dao and Gu, 2024], each memory update traverses the full nonlinear Transformer depth, providing looped-Transformer-like recurrent depth without extra Transformer iterations [Dehghani et al., 2019, Giannou et al., 2023]. Because every tokens decoder state serves as memory through its ordinary K/V entry, the recurrence also requires no dedicated memory tokens or cache and introduces no artificial segment or block boundaries [Dai et al., 2019, Rae et al., 2020, Hutchins et al., 2022, Bulatov et al., 2022]. Bounded recurrent inference. The token and memory windows remain fixed as the sequence grows. As in sliding-window attention [Beltagy et al., 2020, Jiang et al., 2023], inference uses bounded local KV cache; the recurrent memories carry information beyond that window without increasing its size. Parallel large-scale pretraining. Although inference is recurrent, ideally pretraining should process all positions in parallel, preserving standard Transformer throughput [Vaswani et al., 2017]. Achieving this parallelism is nontrivial for nonlinear recurrence [Lim et al., 2024, Gonzalez et al., 2024]. The interface provides the first two properties by construction: it writes mt at every position while keeping both conditioning windows fixed. Parallel pretraining, however, is not automatic. Text provides x1:T but not the latent trajectory m1:T ; because each update consumes preceding memories, direct training must generate this trajectory sequentially. The central question is how to preserve the recurrent interface at deployment without unrolling it during pretraining. Maglev: parallel supervision for recurrent memory. Maglev breaks this dependency by separating memory construction during pretraining from memory propagation at inference. stronger causal prefiller produces target memories 1:T from the observed sequence in parallel. sliding-window decoder consumes the shifted targets 0:T 1, predicts the next tokens, and emits memories m1:T . consistency loss aligns each mt with t, teaching to produce the memory needed at the next step. Training therefore requires two sequence-parallel passes. At inference, is removed and closes the loop with its own memories. Figure 1 illustrates the architecture. The deployed decoder remains close to an ordinary slidingwindow Transformer, augmenting the same local attention pattern with gated K/V pathway for shifted recurrent memory. The decoders final normalized state is both the memory mt and the input to the language-modeling head. Fixed token and memory windows keep inference costs bounded. Contributions. We propose token-wise nonlinear recurrent-memory Transformer that folds shifted memories into sliding-window K/V entries, preserving bounded inference without extra memory tokens. We introduce lifted parallel training, where causal prefiller generates targets in parallel and consistency training teaches decoder to reproduce them without sequential recurrent 2 unrolling. With 435M-scale deployed decoder trained on 43.52B tokens, our best model improves FineWeb-Edu validation BPB from 0.7413 to 0.7251 and average downstream accuracy from 54.1 to 56.4 over matched sliding-window Transformer, while also outperforming matched latent recurrent Transformer. Moreover, and can share most parameters while preserving most gains.

sections.title: 3 Related Work
sections.content: Efficient and long-context attention. Transformers rely on softmax attention over past tokens [Vaswani et al., 2017]. Long-context variants reduce this cost with local attention, compressed memory, recurrence, retrieval, or hybrid memory mechanisms. Transformer-XL and Compressive Transformers reuse or compress segment-level activations [Dai et al., 2019, Rae et al., 2020]; Infiniattention and landmark-style methods add compressed or random-access memory for longer contexts [Munkhdalai et al., 2024, Mohtashami and Jaggi, 2023]; Memorizing Transformers augment attention with external retrieval [Wu et al., 2022]. Sliding-window attention is especially practical because it bounds compute and cache size, but it drops information outside the window. Maglev keeps the sliding window and adds shifted memory that carries information forward through the decoder. Linear recurrent and convolutional sequence models. Linear attention and state space models replace the full key-value cache with fixed-size recurrent state [Katharopoulos et al., 2020, Gu et al., 2022, Gu and Dao, 2023, Dao and Gu, 2024]. Related convolutional and state-space models such as H3, S5, Hyena, and Mamba use efficient recurrent or convolutional sequence operators [Fu et al., 4 2022, Smith et al., 2022, Poli et al., 2023, Gu and Dao, 2023]. Wavelet-inspired multiresolution convolutional memory instead summarizes the history at exponentially increasing temporal scales using learned filters shared across tree of dilated causal convolutions [Shi et al., 2023]. More recent gated recurrent architectures, including RetNet, RWKV, Griffin/Hawk, gated delta networks, and xLSTM, add data-dependent gates or learned update rules for stronger memory control [Sun et al., 2023, Peng et al., 2023, De et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024, Beck et al., 2024]. These approaches are efficient, but their memory transformations are typically linear, affine, or specialized recurrent or convolutional operators. Maglev also uses bounded state, but its state is produced by nonlinear Transformer decoder and trained through prefiller consistency; unlike multiresolution convolutional memory, its state size does not grow with the number of temporal scales. Hybrid attention and recurrence. Hybrid models combine local attention with recurrent or statespace layers so recent tokens remain easy to access while older context is compressed [De et al., 2024, Ren et al., 2024, Lieber et al., 2024]. Feedback Transformers and TransformerFAM expose high-level past representations to future computation [Fan et al., 2021, Hwang et al., 2024]; Recurrent Memory Transformers and Block-Recurrent Transformers carry memory tokens or block states across segments [Bulatov et al., 2022, Hutchins et al., 2022]; block-state and retention-style models balance recurrence and parallelism through blockwise computation [Pilault et al., 2023, Sun et al., 2023]. Maglev shares the goal of bounded memory, but keeps the deployed model close to sliding-window Transformer by injecting shifted memory through the decoders K/V pathway. Online and test-time memory. Several recent works view sequence models as online learners or test-time memory systems [Liu et al., 2024b, Sun et al., 2024, Behrouz et al., 2024]. Other work studies how to parallelize nonlinear recurrent computation [Lim et al., 2024, Gonzalez et al., 2024]. Maglev is closest in spirit to this line because its recurrent update is nonlinear, but it avoids sequential training by learning from parallel prefiller rather than by directly unrolling the decoder recurrence. Latent recurrence and extra computation. Depth-recurrent and latent-thinking methods add computation by looping blocks or inserting auxiliary tokens before prediction [Dehghani et al., 2019, Giannou et al., 2023, Geiping et al., 2026, Goyal et al., 2024, Pfau et al., 2024, Herel and Mikolov, 2024, Zelikman et al., 2024, Hao et al., 2024]. Concurrently, LRT [Huang et al., 2026] passes previous-token memory state into the next token and trains this recurrence through parallel refinement passes. Other concurrent work also uses parallel supervision for recurrent memory: Supervised Memory Training [Kumar and Isola, 2026] trains general RNNs from Transformergenerated memory labels, while Rec2PM [Chen et al., 2026] trains compact preference-memory updates for long-sequence generative recommendation. Maglev applies similar idea to languagemodeling Transformers: it injects shifted token memories through the K/V pathway, retaining the attention-window and cache profile of ordinary sliding-window attention while carrying richer recurrent state. It also supports sharing parameters between the prefiller and decoder , tying the parallel training signal directly to the recurrent Transformer rather than using fully separate teacherstudent system.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate Maglev in the nanochat pretraining stack [Karpathy, 2025]. All models use the same tokenizer, data pipeline, optimizer family, sequence length, and evaluation scripts; architecturespecific differences are described below. Training setup. We use the d20 nanochat architecture: = 20 layers, width = 1280, head dimension 128, 10 attention heads, and maximum sequence length 2048. The short-window size is = 512. The standard d20 model has 435,159,040 non-embedding scaling parameters, and we train for 43.52B tokens, corresponding to 100 Chinchilla-style token budget when embedding parameters are excluded [Hoffmann et al., 2022]. The optimizer batch contains 524,288 tokens per step, and we use the MuonAdamW training recipe [Jordan et al., 2024]. Models. We evaluate sharedparameter Maglev and separate-parameter variant, each with consistency weight λ {0.1, 1.0}. Evaluation. We report FineWeb-Edu validation bits per byte (FW BPB) [Lozhkov et al., 2024], LAMBADA perplexity and accuracy [Paperno et al., 2016], and common pretraining downstream benchmarks: PIQA [Bisk et al., 2020], HellaSwag [Zellers et al., 2019], WinoGrande [Sakaguchi et al., 2021], ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge [Clark et al., 2018], SocialIQA [Sap et al., 2019], and BoolQ [Clark et al., 2019]. The average column is the mean of the reported downstream accuracies. Results. Maglev improves the fixed-window decoder without relying on full attention at inference. The shared Maglev model with λ = 0.1 reaches 0.7295 FW BPB and 56.2 average downstream accuracy, improving over both the SSSS sliding-window baseline and the corresponding LRT baseline. The separate-parameter variant with λ = 1 gives the best FW BPB (0.7251) and average downstream score (56.4). The comparison suggests that additional prefiller capacity can improve the consistency target, while the shared model uses less parameter memory and keeps the two paths tightly coupled. The results also show that the consistency weight is not purely monotone. larger λ improves the separate-parameter model, but hurts the shared model on several downstream tasks. This is consistent with the role of Q: when and share most parameters, an overly strong memory-consistency term can constrain the decoder representation; when has separate capacity, the stronger target can provide more useful training signal.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: We introduced Maglev, fixed-memory recurrent Transformer trained through prefillerdecoder consistency objective. The prefiller provides parallel memory targets t, while the decoder learns to predict tokens and produce its own memories mt using sliding-window attention with recurrent K/V injection. At inference, the prefiller is removed and the decoder runs as bounded-memory recurrent model. Our experiments show that this scheme improves validation BPB and downstream pretraining benchmarks over sliding-window and LRT baselines in the nanochat d20 setting. More broadly, Maglev provides way to train nonlinear recurrent model with fixed inference memory while preserving parallel training. Because our experiments were constrained by available compute, Maglev remains preliminary investigation rather than definitive study of this design space. Several directions remain open. First, scaling Maglev will require studying the tradeoff between prefiller strength and decoder capacity, together with kernels that make recurrent injection efficient in deployment. Second, need not be trained from scratch with : pretrained or lightly fine-tuned language model could provide memory targets while only is trained, distilling its representations into compact recurrent decoder. Third, our results show that substantial sharing between and is possible, but the best sharing pattern remains unclear; intermediate designs could share embeddings, MLPs, attention projections, or selected layers while retaining task-specific components. Finally, recurrent K/V injection is only one way to expose past memories. Future work should compare alternatives such as residual-stream injection, recurrent tokens, cross-attention, and layer-specific memory projections, characterizing their tradeoffs in expressivity, stability, parameter cost, cache size, and inference throughput.
